questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}+{y}^{2}),$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ exists.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2} & >0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}>0\}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2} & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ is defined only when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y)=1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ is defined only when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.
$$

- The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z),$ find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂z}$ exists.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & >0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0\}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $z$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)}{x+y},$ find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂z}$ exists.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}z & >0\,\text{and}\,x+y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0\}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+y}\cdot \frac{1}{z} \\  & =\frac{1}{z(x+y)}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}z(x+y) & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $z$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0\}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{z+y-{x}^{2}}?$

I. The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(0,0,1)$

II. ${f}_{y}(1,2,0)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{z}(1,1,0)$ is defined
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{x}{\sqrt{z+y-{x}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z+y-{x}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z+y-{x}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,0,1)=\sqrt{1+0-{0}^{2}}=1,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(0,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,0,1) & =-\frac{0}{\sqrt{1+0-{0}^{2}}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,2,0)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,2,0)=\sqrt{0+2-{1}^{2}}=1,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,2,0) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{0+2-{1}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1,0)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,1,0)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{0+1-{1}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II only'.
